title: A New Initial Distribution for Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks to Load Probability Distributions
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a novel method using classical label replacement to generate initial distributions for quantum GAN generators that can be implemented with shallow quantum circuits (single-qubit gates, achievable at depth d=0/1). Simulation results show this approach improves learning efficiency and accuracy when loading target distributions (notably log-normal, triangular, and bimodal) compared with uniform initializations and can outperform deeper-circuit normal initializations for important finance-related distributions, aiding quantum expectation estimation workflows.
methodology_description: The authors propose a classical label-replacement method to produce useful initial probability distributions for quantum Generative Adversarial Networks (qGANs) while keeping quantum circuits shallow (single-qubit gates only in the Init block). The method (Algorithm 1) sorts the target discrete probability mass, computes cumulative ratios, and maps those ratios to Ry rotation angles so that a shallow quantum circuit followed by a classical relabeling of measurement outcomes approximates a chosen target distribution. They integrate this Init into a parameterized quantum generator (repeated layers of single-qubit Ry rotations and CZ entangling gates) and train the qGAN in simulation. Training uses a classical discriminator (PyTorch) and the parameter-shift rule to obtain gradients of the quantum generator. The experimental evaluation compares three initializations (their method, uniform, and a normal-based Init) on three synthetic target distributions (log-normal, triangular, bimodal) discretized to 8 points (3 qubits). qGAN training used AMSGRAD (lr=1e-4, beta1=0.7, beta2=0.99), the non-saturating GAN loss, 2000 training epochs, and repeated experiments (10 independent runs) for robustness. Performance is measured by relative entropy (KL divergence) between target and generated discrete distributions.
algorithms_used: Parameter-shift rule for quantum gradient estimation
experimental_setup: Classical simulation of quantum circuits using Qiskit (no real QPU). Generator circuits were 3-qubit (8-point discretization) with an Init block implemented using single-qubit Ry rotations plus classical label replacement. Parameterized generator layers comprised Ry rotations and CZ entanglers; tested layer counts k={1,2,3}. Discriminator implemented in PyTorch (50-node input layer, 20-node hidden layer, 1-node output). Parameter-shift gradients computed using 8000 samples; training used AMSGRAD (lr=1e-4, beta1=0.7, beta2=0.99), up to 2000 epochs, 10 independent runs per setting.
dataset_used: Synthetic distributions only: (1) Log-normal with mean µ=1 and standard deviation σ=1; (2) Triangular with lower limit l=0, upper limit u=7, mode m=2; (3) Bimodal mixture of two Gaussians with µ1=0.5, σ1=1 and µ2=3.5, σ2=0.5. No real financial datasets were used.

experiment_input.source: synthetic sampling from the analytic target distributions
experiment_input.size: 2000 samples drawn from each target distribution for training data
experiment_input.preprocessing: Samples discretized into 8 bins (3 qubits). Mini-batch size = 2000 real samples per discriminator batch; 2000 generated samples measured from the generator were added per batch.

steps: For a chosen target distribution, sample 2000 real data points and discretize into 8 classes.
Compute Init Ry angles via label replacement (Algorithm 1): sort target probabilities, compute cumulative sums/ratios, map to Ry angles (θi = 2 arccos(ri)).
Construct quantum generator: Init circuit (single-qubit Ry on each qubit) followed by k repetitions of parameterized layers (Ry on each qubit + CZ entanglers).
Initialize generator parameters uniformly in [-1e-1, 1e-1] (except Init which may be set according to method under test).
Construct classical discriminator (PyTorch): input layer 50 nodes, hidden 20 nodes, output 1 node.
Train qGAN up to 2000 epochs using AMSGRAD (lr=1e-4, beta1=0.7, beta2=0.99) and non-saturating GAN losses. For generator gradients use the parameter-shift rule with 8000 samples.
Each discriminator update uses 2000 real + 2000 generated samples.
Evaluate generated discrete distribution at intervals using relative entropy (KL divergence) to the target.
Repeat experiment 10 independent times per initialisation and per k in {1,2,3}.
parameters_tuned_or_tested: Number of parameterized layer repetitions k ∈ {1,2,3}
Initialization method: proposed label-replacement, uniform (Hadamards), normal-based Init

experiment_output.format: Tabulated relative entropy (KL divergence) statistics across 10 runs per setting (mean, standard deviation, minimum) plus plots of generated vs target discrete PMFs for best runs.
metrics: Relative entropy (KL divergence) between target and generated discrete distributions
baselines: Normal-distribution based Init (as in prior work)

experiment_parameters.loss_functions: Non-saturating GAN loss (standard generator and discriminator losses)

hardware_details.notes: All quantum experiments were performed in classical simulation (Qiskit). No real QPU or cloud quantum device was used.

key_findings: [supported] The authors propose a classical label-replacement method to produce a variety of initial probability distributions for the qGAN generator using only single-qubit gates, enabling implementation with shallow circuits (d=1 and interpretable as d=0 via composition into generator weights).

[supported] In simulations (3 qubits / 8-point discretization) the proposed initial distribution yields substantially lower relative entropy (better fit) than a uniform single-qubit initial distribution across the tested targets (log-normal, triangular, bimodal).
[supported] For the log-normal target, the proposed method outperforms a normal-distribution initialisation (which requires deeper / multi-qubit gates) in the reported simulations.

[supported] The proposed initial distribution can be interpreted as initial generator weights because Ry rotations compose (Ry(θ1)Ry(θ2) = Ry(θ1+θ2)), so the Init circuit angles can be folded into generator parameters (i.e., implementable at d=0).

[speculative] The method is claimed to be advantageous for NISQ devices compared to using a normal-distribution initialisation because it avoids two-qubit gates and deeper circuits (thus less noisy), though this is argued rather than experimentally demonstrated on noisy hardware.

[speculative] The authors argue their approach is robust to scaling in qubit number because the Init construction stays at shallow depth; however, the paper does not present empirical results beyond the small-scale (8-point / 3-qubit) simulations.

[supported] The authors successfully generate approximations of log-normal, triangular, and bimodal distributions more efficiently (in their metric of relative entropy) than uniform initialisation in their simulated qGAN training runs.

[speculative] The paper asserts that using a distribution 'near' the target (via label replacement) improves qGAN learning efficiency in general; this is supported by their simulations but generalisation beyond tested distributions/qubit counts is left for future work.
results_summary: The paper introduces a classical label-replacement technique to craft initial distributions for quantum GAN generators using only single-qubit rotations, which can be folded into generator weights. In simulated qGAN training on 3-qubit (8-point) targets (log-normal, triangular, bimodal), the proposed initialisation consistently produces lower relative-entropy fits than a uniform single-qubit initialisation and outperforms a normal-distribution initialisation for the log-normal target. The method is claimed to be shallow (d=1 or effectively d=0) and potentially advantageous for NISQ devices because it avoids multi-qubit gates, but scaling and noisy-hardware benefits are not empirically demonstrated beyond the presented small-scale simulations.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper frames the work as improving the shallow-circuit state-preparation step needed for quantum expectation estimation (which underlies quantum speedups in amplitude estimation). However, it does not demonstrate an end-to-end quantum computational advantage on hardware or in noisy simulations; the contribution is a theoretical/engineering improvement to a subroutine (state loading) that could help realize quantum advantage in future systems.
limitations: Evaluations were limited to three target distributions (log-normal, triangular, bimodal); generality to other distributions was not demonstrated (author-stated).
Scalability with increasing number of qubits was not assessed; the method was demonstrated on a small discretization (8 points / 3 qubits) (author-stated).
The impact of the number of measurements (shots) and the number of generator parameters (weights) on accuracy was not evaluated (author-stated).
All experiments were performed via classical simulation (qiskit simulator); no experiments on real noisy NISQ hardware were reported (explicit).
Code and datasets are not publicly available (available only on request), limiting immediate reproducibility (explicit).

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — A classical label-replacement method produces useful initial probability distributions mapped to single-qubit Ry rotations, enabling very shallow Init circuits (d=0/1) that are interpretable as NISQ-friendly.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The approach is hybrid: classical preprocessing (label replacement and discretization) plus a parameterized quantum generator trained with a classical discriminator using parameter-shift gradients.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — In 3-qubit (8-bin) Qiskit simulations the proposed Init yields consistently lower KL divergence (better fit) vs uniform (Hadamard) and vs a deeper normal-based Init across log-normal, triangular, and bimodal targets.
#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments were performed in classical simulation (Qiskit); no experiments on real QPUs or noisy-device emulation were reported.
#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstrations are limited to 3 qubits / 8 discrete bins; scalability to higher-resolution or high-dimensional financial distributions is not shown.
#limitation:noise — The paper does not evaluate performance under realistic device noise or employ error-mitigation, so NISQ claims are not validated on hardware.

#limitation:data-encoding — Method relies on discretization and classical relabeling to map distributions to basis states; costs and fidelity of encoding continuous or high-dimensional financial data are not addressed.
